# Cortical Flattening and the Marching Cubes Algorithm

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

The previous chapter built a 3D mesh representation of the cortical surface
and introduced flat maps as a way to display data on that surface. This
chapter works through the two computational methods that make that possible:
flattening, which maps the 3D mesh onto a 2D plane, and marching
cubes/marching squares, the general algorithm for extracting a surface (or a
boundary curve, in 2D) from classified volumetric data in the first place.

## Flattening the cortical surface

Gray-matter nodes on the cortical mesh have 3D positions $(x, y, z)$; the goal
of flattening is to assign each node a 2D position $(u, v)$ in an image plane
while preserving, as much as possible, the neighborhood relations of the
original mesh. The method used here follows a principle developed by W.T.
Tutte (1960): place each node at the average position of its connected
neighbors, and no folds are introduced into the surface this way
(@fig-ch68-flattening-tutte-principle; @tutte1963-drawgraph).

![Flattening a cortical mesh follows Tutte's principle: place each node at
the average position of its connected
neighbors.](images/ch68/flattening-tutte-principle.png){#fig-ch68-flattening-tutte-principle}

The important practical point is that this averaging condition is a *linear*
system. If $\mathbf{X}$ holds the 2D positions of the interior nodes and
$\mathbf{X}_0$ the fixed positions of the perimeter nodes, the condition that
each interior node sits at the average of its neighbors is written
$\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{N}\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}_0$, where
$\mathbf{N}$ is a node-connection matrix (normalized by each node's number of
connections) and $\mathbf{P}$ plays the same role for perimeter connections.
Solving for $\mathbf{X}$ gives $\mathbf{X} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{N})^{-1}
\mathbf{P}\mathbf{X}_0$ — a single linear solve places every interior node at
once, in a way that preserves the mesh's topology
(@fig-ch68-flattening-matrix-linear-equation).

![The matrix form of the flattening equation: node positions are found by
solving one linear
system.](images/ch68/flattening-matrix-linear-equation.png){#fig-ch68-flattening-matrix-linear-equation}

In practice, once a segmentation exists, flattening a patch of cortex is
straightforward: select a start point on the mesh, select a distance (radius)
defining how much of the mesh to unfold, and run the algorithm
(@fig-ch68-flattening-tools-steps). Tools such as `mrFlatMesh` implement this
directly: they read in the gray-matter mesh, take a start point and a radius,
and solve the flattening equations
(@fig-ch68-mrflatmesh-gui).

![Flattening tools: given a segmentation, select a start point and a radius,
then run the
algorithm.](images/ch68/flattening-tools-steps.png){#fig-ch68-flattening-tools-steps}

![`mrFlatMesh`: a graphical tool for flattening a patch of the gray-matter
mesh.](images/ch68/mrflatmesh-gui.png){#fig-ch68-mrflatmesh-gui}

The result can be inspected directly: the mesh triangles end up on the plane
without any edge crossings, confirming the flattening is valid, though the
triangles are not uniformly positioned across the flattened patch
(@fig-ch68-examining-flattened-mesh). Two further quantities are typically
computed and displayed alongside the flattened mesh: a manifold distance map
(geodesic distance from the starting point, measured along the original
surface) and a curvature map, which together let a viewer judge how much the
flattening has distorted the true surface (@fig-ch68-measuring-distances-curvature).

![Examining the flattened mesh: triangles land on the plane without edge
crossings, though unevenly
spaced.](images/ch68/examining-flattened-mesh.png){#fig-ch68-examining-flattened-mesh}

![Measuring distances (a manifold distance map) and showing curvature,
computed alongside the flattened
mesh.](images/ch68/measuring-distances-curvature.png){#fig-ch68-measuring-distances-curvature}

## Marching squares: finding a boundary curve

Both flattening and mesh construction depend on a more basic operation:
extracting a boundary (in 2D) or a surface (in 3D) from a classified grid of
samples. In two dimensions this is the marching squares algorithm. Each grid
node is classified as inside or outside the shape (green vertices inside,
in this illustration); new vertices are placed at the midpoint of each
in/out pair of neighboring grid nodes (red), and the boundary is drawn
through those new vertices.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Classified grid

![A regular grid of sample points classified as inside (green) or outside a
shape.](images/ch68/marching-squares-grid-vertices.png){#fig-ch68-marching-squares-1}

## Drawing the boundary

![New vertices (red) are placed at the midpoint of each in/out pair, and the
boundary is drawn through
them.](images/ch68/marching-squares-boundary-line.png){#fig-ch68-marching-squares-2}

## Local configurations

![Only a small number of distinct local line configurations are possible,
each a rotation of one of four basic
cases.](images/ch68/marching-squares-configurations.png){#fig-ch68-marching-squares-3}
:::

The result is an "OK" but visibly jagged representation of the true boundary
— the polygon approximation is more angular than the underlying shape, so
some form of boundary smoothing is required. One simple approach: find the
curve normals at each vertex, smooth the way their orientation changes along
the curve, and reconstruct the curve from the smoothed normals
(@fig-ch68-boundary-smoothing-normals).

![Boundary smoothing: find the curve normals, smooth their orientation
change, and reconstruct the curve from the smoothed
normals.](images/ch68/boundary-smoothing-normals.png){#fig-ch68-boundary-smoothing-normals}

## Marching cubes: finding a surface in 3D

Marching cubes is the natural three-dimensional generalization of marching
squares, and it is the standard algorithm for extracting a surface mesh from
a classified 3D volume such as a segmented gray/white matter
volume (@lorensen1987-marchingcubes). Each cube (formed by eight neighboring
voxel corners) has its corners classified as above or below an isovalue;
since there are 8 corners, there are $2^8 = 256$ possible corner
classifications, and the algorithm must determine which section (or
sections) of surface divides each cube accordingly.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Classifying cube corners

![Each of a cube's 8 corners is classified as inside or outside the
isosurface, giving 256 possible
configurations.](images/ch68/marching-cubes-corner-classification.png){#fig-ch68-marching-cubes-1}

## The 15 distinct cube combinations

![After removing trivial (all-in or all-out) cases, 15 distinct surface
configurations remain; edge-intersection points determine how the surface
cuts through each
cube.](images/ch68/marching-cubes-15-combinations.png){#fig-ch68-marching-cubes-2}

## Symmetry reduces the cases further

![Rotation about any of the 3 primary axes, mirroring, and corner-state
inversion relate many of the 15 combinations to each other, so only a
handful of truly distinct cases must be handled
explicitly.](images/ch68/marching-cubes-symmetry-reduction.png){#fig-ch68-marching-cubes-3}
:::

Increasing the point-sampling density improves the smoothness of the
resulting mesh but does not, by itself, solve the fundamental jaggedness
problem — the surface is still built from flat triangular facets, just more
of them (@fig-ch68-point-sampling-density).

![Increasing point-sampling density improves resolution but does not solve
the fundamental faceting
problem.](images/ch68/point-sampling-density.png){#fig-ch68-point-sampling-density}

## Connectivity, revisited

Both marching squares and marching cubes depend on a definition of
neighborhood connectivity among voxels, the same issue raised in the previous
chapter's discussion of white-matter topology. In 3D, the two common
conventions are 6-connectivity (only face-adjacent neighbors) and
26-connectivity (all face-, edge-, and corner-adjacent neighbors)
(@fig-ch68-connectivity-6-26-neighborhood). The choice of connectivity
convention affects which configurations are treated as topologically valid
and is part of why the Euler-number bookkeeping introduced earlier matters in
practice, not just in principle.

![Common types of voxel connectivity: 6-neighborhood (face-adjacent only)
versus 26-neighborhood (face, edge, and corner
adjacent).](images/ch68/connectivity-6-26-neighborhood.png){#fig-ch68-connectivity-6-26-neighborhood}
